text:
The Case for the Joined-Up Line

Every few years a headline announces the death of handwriting. Keyboards are everywhere, the argument goes, so children should spend their precious classroom hours on typing, coding and other skills that look more like the future. Some education systems have already moved in that direction. Finland dropped compulsory cursive from its national curriculum in 2016, and several American states let it lapse before a number of them restored it. The question is a fair one. Time in a primary school day is scarce, and nobody should defend a tradition merely because it is old. But when I weigh what joined-up handwriting costs against what it gives, I conclude that primary schools should keep teaching it, and teach it well.

Begin with what the skill actually is. Joined-up handwriting is not decoration. It is a method of writing in which the pen stays on the page for the length of a word, so that the hand moves in one continuous motion instead of a series of stabs. That single design feature is the whole point. A child who prints must lift the pen between every letter, deciding afresh each time where to place it next. A child who joins letters learns the shape of a word as a unit, with its rhythm and its internal logic. The movement is faster once learned, and it is less tiring, because the hand glides instead of restarting. Teachers who have watched a class graduate from laboured print to a fluent running hand know the change is real. Writing stops being a task of construction and starts to become a vehicle for thought.

That brings me to the strongest argument, which is about thinking. Writing by hand is a bottleneck for many young children, and the bottleneck is not neutral. When forming letters demands all of a child's attention, little attention remains for spelling, sentence structure or the idea she is trying to express. Researchers have noted for years that handwriting fluency predicts the quality and length of children's compositions. Children who write automatically produce more, and better, text, because the mechanical effort has dropped out of working memory and left room for content. The aim of teaching joined writing is therefore not beauty. It is automaticity. A fluent joined hand is one of the quickest routes to that state, because the connected movement removes the pen lifts that slow a printer down.

Skeptics reply that typing offers automaticity too, and that is partly true. But typing is not available to small children in the way a pencil is. Fine motor control of the fingers on a keyboard is poor in a six year old, touch typing takes months of dedicated practice to reach useful speed, and devices bring costs, charging, breakages and inequality of access. A pencil works in every classroom, on every desk, in every weather and in every household. It does not crash. It does not distract a child with notifications. In a world where schools are rightly worried about screen time, a skill that lets children produce extended written work without a screen is an asset to protect.

There is also growing evidence that the physical act of handwriting does something for learning that keystrokes do not. Studies using brain imaging have found that handwriting engages wider networks than typing does, particularly for young children learning letters. Experiments with students taking notes have suggested, with the usual caveats about replication, that those who write by hand tend to process lectures more deeply, because they cannot transcribe everything and must summarise as they go. I would not rest the entire case on these findings, since the research is mixed and some of it is overstated in popular coverage. Still, the direction of the evidence is consistent enough that abandoning the skill on the assumption that nothing is lost looks reckless. The burden of proof belongs with those who want to remove a long-standing practice, not with those who want to keep it.

The most telling objection is that print is good enough. Why teach a second script, when a clear printed hand serves every purpose? Here I think the defenders of print overlook the cost of the middle route that many schools now take, which is to teach print and then leave children to invent their own joins. What happens in practice is that pupils drift into a private hybrid, half printed and half scribbled, with no model for how letters ought to connect. Handwriting in secondary school and in adult life is often an unreadable mess, and the cause is that nobody ever taught the efficient version. Joined-up writing, taught systematically, gives children a good design to start from. They may later personalise it, and most will, but they will personalise something sound rather than improvise something broken.

Consider too what it means for children who struggle. Dyslexic pupils and those with dyspraxia are often cited as people for whom cursive is a burden, and some individuals do find it hard. But a number of specialists argue the opposite for many such children. Because every letter in a joined script starts from a consistent point on the line and flows in a single direction, the movements are repetitive and learnable, and reversals like b and d become less common when the child forms each by a distinct stroke sequence. Printing offers more opportunities for those reversals, since the letters share a stick and a ball in different arrangements. Of course some children will need alternatives, and a good school makes those available without hesitation. The existence of exceptions argues for support, not for abolishing the default.

A further point concerns the way a joined script connects children to the written world. Adults do not only read print. They read handwritten notes from relatives, historical documents, inscriptions in old books, labels on family photographs, letters from grandparents. A child who cannot read joined writing is cut off from this material, and the cut is silent, because the child may not realise what is missing. Archivists and teachers already report that some students cannot read the handwriting of earlier generations. Teaching joined script is a small act of cultural literacy, a way of ensuring that the documents of the past remain open to the young. It is also a plain practical matter on exam day, when children in most systems still write by hand for hours and need a pace they can sustain.

I do not want to pretend that the traditional approach is beyond criticism. Too many schools have taught joining as a drill in neatness, with endless copying of letter patterns, ruled lines and teachers who mark down children for slanting the wrong way. That is a poor way to treat a skill whose purpose is fluency. Handwriting lessons should be short, frequent and purposeful. Ten minutes of focused daily practice beats an hour of copying once a week. Children should learn the joins in the context of real words and real sentences about things that interest them, not isolated exercises. Teachers should care about legibility and speed, not about conformity to a single house style. And schools should be honest that handwriting is one part of a wider writing curriculum that also includes typing, so that children leave primary school able to do both.

Notice that this is a more modest claim than the one the nostalgic make. I am not saying that handwriting is a moral discipline, or that neat cursive reveals character, or that the world was better when everyone wrote copperplate. I am saying that a particular skill, taught for a modest amount of time in the early years, repays the investment many times over. It frees working memory, supports composition, avoids dependence on devices, protects access to the written record and gives children an efficient hand for life. The cost is perhaps a few hours across a school year, a sliver of the primary timetable. Set against the benefits, that is cheap.

The future that the abolitionists point to will certainly contain keyboards, and it will contain voice and whatever comes after voice. Nobody sensible disputes that children must learn to type. But the choice has been presented too starkly, as if every minute given to the pen is a minute stolen from the screen. Children can and should learn both, in the right order. Handwriting comes first, because it is the one that small hands can do, and because the fluency it builds carries over into everything else a young writer will attempt. Taught well, the joined-up line is not a relic. It is one of the most efficient tools a child will ever be given for turning thoughts into words, and primary schools would be foolish to take it away.
